source.title: What Language Model Architecture and Pretraining Objective Work Best for Zero-Shot Generalization?
source.authors: Thomas Wang; Adam Roberts; Daniel Hesslow; Teven Le Scao; Hyung Won Chung; Iz Beltagy; Julien Launay; Colin A. Raffel

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates downstream zero-shot performance at multiple pretraining-token checkpoints, a different measure from the loss-scaling laws in the claim. It does not fit scaling laws or test compute-optimal allocation.
record.gate_note: The paper reports zero-shot accuracy and validation-loss adaptation results, but does not test held-out pretraining loss against parameter count, tokens, or compute, nor fit small-run predictions. Its scaling-relevant result is a downstream-performance comparison across pretraining-token checkpoints (Figure 8). References to scaling-law work are background citations, not results from those studies.
record.test_reason: The study compares architectures and objectives at one fixed scale: about 5B and 11B parameters, 168B tokens, about 15 PF-days. It fits no loss–scale relation and tests no compute-optimal split. Scaling-law papers such as Hoffmann et al. are cited only as background. Its only multi-scale data are three pretraining checkpoints (42B, 84B, 168B tokens) per configuration, used to show that architecture ranking is stable. That is not a test of whether downstream performance improves predictably with scale or loss. The validation-loss curves in Figure 6 compare adaptation against from-scratch training on different objectives, not loss against scale. Architecture differences are measured on zero-shot accuracy, not held-out loss, so V4 is not tested either.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is correct but incomplete. The authors conclude that CD:FLM is best for zero-shot use right after pretraining, and ED:MLM is best after multitask finetuning. They also find that adaptation converts efficiently between these setups. LM adaptation of a non-causal MLM model gives a 1.6× speedup. Non-causal MLM adaptation of a causal FLM model gives a 3.3× speedup and second-best post-finetuning performance. They therefore recommend CD:FLM pretraining followed by non-causal MLM adaptation, then multitask finetuning.
record.recipe_differences: Compares architectures and pretraining objectives using downstream zero-shot accuracy; it does not reproduce loss-scaling fits or compute-optimal allocation analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: Architecture, pretraining objective, multitask-finetuning status, benchmark and prompt choice affect reported zero-shot results. The paper reports that dropout during multitask finetuning also changes performance.

fits_no_version.finding: After multitask finetuning, the ranking of architecture/objective configurations on T0-Eval stays largely unchanged across the 42B, 84B and 168B-token checkpoints. ED:MLM at a quarter of the tokens already exceeds the others' final scores (Figure 8; Table 8).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The ranking of architecture/objective choices on downstream zero-shot accuracy is stable across pretraining checkpoints.

record.problems: The scaling-relevant result concerns downstream accuracy rather than held-out pretraining loss. The checkpoint comparison does not fit a predictive curve or report exact Figure 8 values in the text. Evaluation is limited to the stated model configurations, token amounts, and benchmarks.
record.rows_left_out: Tables and figures comparing fixed-checkpoint zero-shot scores across architectures/objectives were not recorded as scale results. Adaptation validation-loss curves and speedup comparisons (Section 5, Figure 6) concern changing objectives and adaptation, not loss scaling with model size, training tokens, or compute. Other per-checkpoint series in Figure 8 are represented only by the explicitly stated aggregate comparison in r1.

untested.parts: No held-out loss against parameters, tokens or compute; no power-law fit.
Architectures are compared at matched compute on zero-shot accuracy, not held-out loss. Depth and width are not varied at fixed parameter count.
Text pretraining only; no other modality. Fine-tuning is not analysed for scaling.
No predictive fit of downstream performance on scale or loss. Only three token checkpoints per run.
No fitted exponents or fitting choices examined.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6 'supports' label is dropped. The study has no results on scaling laws as defined. Table 8 text extraction is garbled, so per-checkpoint values cannot be reliably aligned with configurations.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not measure held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute, or test a power-law form.
The study does not fit losses on small runs and compare predictions with much larger runs.
The study does not search for a loss-minimising parameter/token split at fixed compute or estimate allocation exponents.
It compares architectures on zero-shot accuracy, not on whether architectural changes have only slight effects on held-out loss.
The study is about text language models and does not test whether loss power laws generalise to other modalities or the listed training regimes.
It reports downstream zero-shot accuracy across pretraining-token checkpoints, but does not fit a predictive relationship, extrapolate from small runs, or relate task performance to pretraining loss.
The study varies architecture, objective, and evaluation setup, but does not assess how fitted loss exponents or compute-optimal allocations depend on setup or fitting choices.

rows.subject: ED:MLM (encoder-decoder pretrained with masked language modeling)
rows.stage_stated: 168B-token pretraining checkpoints followed by 13B-token multitask finetuning; Figure 8 shows increasing pretraining amounts
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated zero-shot performance across increasing amounts of pretraining tokens after multitask finetuning.

conditions.value: increasing pretraining tokens; Figure 8 plots checkpoint progression

rows.baseline: Other architecture/objective configurations' final performance; random baseline 41.7
rows.value: Figure only; authors state the best model is already above the other configurations' final performance with a quarter of the pretraining tokens.
rows.note: The paper also states that the ordering of configurations does not change significantly throughout pretraining. Exact plotted values are not stated in the accompanying text.
rows.check: This row records an architecture/objective comparison: ED:MLM beats other configurations' final T0-Eval score with a quarter of the tokens, and the ordering is stable. It does not measure whether downstream performance improves predictably with scale or pretraining loss. Three checkpoints of single runs, with no fit or loss relation, cannot show V6's predictability. The V6 link and the 'observed' state are unsupported.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
